etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English benethe, from Old English bineoþan (“beneath, under, below”), equivalent to be- +‎ neath. Cognate with Low German benedden (“beneath”), Dutch beneden (“beneath, under, down”), obsolete German benieden (“below”).

quote.citation: 2013 May 11, “The climate of Tibet: Pole-land”, in The Economist‎[1], volume 407, number 8835, page 80:
quote.text: Of all the transitions brought about on the Earth’s surface by temperature change, the melting of ice into water is the starkest. It is binary. And for the land beneath, the air above and the life around, it changes everything.

quote.citation: c. 1606 (date written), William Shakespeare, “The Tragedie of Macbeth”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act IV, scene iii]:
quote.text: Our country sinks beneath the yoke.

quote.citation: 1718, Alexander Pope, epitaph to Nicholas Rowe
quote.text: Beneath a rude and nameless stone he lies.

quote.citation: 1918, W[illiam] B[abington] Maxwell, chapter V, in The Mirror and the Lamp, Indianapolis, Ind.: The Bobbs-Merrill Company, →OCLC:
quote.text: Here, in the transept and choir, where the service was being held, one was conscious every moment of an increasing brightness; colours glowing vividly beneath the circular chandeliers, and the rows of small lights on the choristers' desks flashed and sparkled in front of the boys' faces, deep linen collars, and red neckbands.

definitions.definition: In a position that is lower in rank, dignity, etc.

quote.citation: a. 1730, Francis Atterbury, in The Grub-Street Journal, Volume 1
quote.text: He will do nothing that is beneath his high station.

definitions.definition: Covered up or concealed by something.
